args.focus: {"claude": "post-commitment continuation: traces that already stated an answer inside the thinking but kept deliberating until the cap (17 of 53 truncated bank traces). Find what the model predicts right after its first in-think answer statement in finished vs truncated traces (token log-probs, top-k), and which components push toward reopening the question (\"But\", \"Wait\", \"Alternatively\") instead of confirming and closing.", "ed_a": "hedging episodes: \"maybe\" / \"perhaps\" / \"Alternatively\" are 2-3x denser in truncated traces than in finished ones. Find the components (MLP neurons, heads, residual directions) active at the onset of such reconsideration episodes, test whether they fire on points already settled earlier in the trace, and whether damping them shortens the specific wasteful episodes without hurting finished answers."}

{"claude": "decision formation in truncated traces that never reach an answer: in finished traces, find the point where the model first commits to an option and what precedes it (which options were eliminated, what evidence was stated); in truncated traces of similar questions, find what is missing at the corresponding point. Look for components that mark \"enough evidence to decide\" or that keep an option open, and test whether strengthening the decision signal makes those traces commit to a correct answer (not just stop).", "ed_a": "revisiting settled options: truncated traces deliberate option by option and often return to options they already ruled out or evaluated. Measure how often an option is re-evaluated after an explicit verdict on it, find the components active when the model reopens an option it already judged (heads attending back to the earlier verdict, MLP neurons), and test whether damping them saves tokens without reducing accuracy on finished traces."}

{"claude": "the never-concluding knowledge questions: law and health traces are cut 18 of 23 times, and 35 of the 53 cut traces never state an answer at all. These are not arithmetic: the model deliberates option by option, recalling rules or facts and weighing them, without converging. Find what differs, inside the reasoning, between finished and never-concluding traces of these subjects (how options are eliminated, whether eliminations are kept, whether the question's key fact is ever pinned down), find the components involved, and test whether an edit helps such traces reach a correct answer (not just stop).", "ed_a": "answer statements that do not close the thinking: 18 of the 53 cut traces of the parent state 'the answer is (X)' and still reach the cap. In about half the statement comes mid-trace (19-66% of it); most are hedged ('Thus likely answer is (E)', 'maybe the correct answer is C') and some are firm and followed by re-verification ('The answer is (G). But we must double-check ...'). The parent's wrap-up neuron (L20 n5414) was meant to close after a statement. Find out why it does not here (does its gate fire on hedged statements? what overrides it after firm ones?), and check the parent's 4 regressions on the bank (finished and correct before its edit, cut now). Remember the lesson that closing helps only where the stated answer is likely right: measure how often hedged versus firm mid-trace statements are correct before you act on them."}

{"claude": "Build an edit that is exactly silent where it does not fire, then use it to carry the best-evidenced mechanism. First find a carrier (a neuron, or another place for a gated function) that leaves untouched traces byte-identical in DEV generate passes (count identical traces and first-difference positions). Then put a targeted function on it, for example generation 6's two-finalist commit (the parent's 18 cut bank traces that narrow to two options). Without silence a +3 point mechanism cannot pass selection.", "ed_a": "Answers that are stated inside the thinking and then re-verified until the cap: 18 of the 53 cut bank traces state an answer (10 of them correct) and still reach the cap. The parent's own wrap-up neuron (L20 n5414) handles some such moments; find which ones it misses and why, and repair them. Make the edit exactly silent where it does not fire (see WHAT IT TAKES TO PASS SELECTION): count byte-identical traces in your DEV passes."}

{"claude":"Decision points in MIXED questions (passk file: the same question answered right in some samples and wrong in others). Teacher-force right and wrong samples and probe, at regular points, what the model would answer if forced to answer now (append a short forced-answer suffix and read the option-letter probabilities), to find WHERE in the trace the eventual answer gets decided and whether the deciding step was a low-probability sampled choice that the model itself rates lower than the alternative. If decisions hinge on specific moments (naming a candidate option, accepting or rejecting an option during a sweep), look for a component that could make the model follow its own better-supported option there.","ed_a":"Systematic content slips. Compare the 20 finished-wrong answers on mixed questions (and finished-wrong answers on never-right questions) with right answers to the same or similar questions: is there a recurring, specific failure (e.g. losing a NOT/EXCEPT/LEAST in the question, misreading a quantity or unit, judging an option against the wrong criterion, rejecting the right option for a stated but false reason)? Find the internal correlate (a direction or component active when the slip happens or when the question contains the trigger) and repair that one failure. Check its coverage on a random sample of practice questions before investing passes."}

{"claude": "EARLY OPTION JUDGEMENT on MIXED questions (passk file: same question right in some samples, wrong in others). Generation 10 showed the conclusion forms gradually and is fixed before the finalists are named, so look EARLIER: in the option-by-option sweep, how does the model judge each option (accept / reject / keep as possible), and where do wrong samples diverge from right samples of the same question? Probe per-option verdicts in read passes (e.g. append a short forced verdict like 'So option (X) is' after the paragraph that discusses X and read the probabilities of correct/incorrect/plausible, or read the forced answer right after each option paragraph), on right and wrong samples of the same question. Look for a SYSTEMATIC, content-independent reason wrong samples reject the right option (e.g. options judged early are rejected more harshly, a criterion applied asymmetrically, a stated but false fact) and for its internal correlate; then repair that one bias and show in a read pass on the SAME texts that the per-option verdict moves. Traces longer than 4,096 tokens: truncate them (probes are prefixes).",
 "ed_a": "MENTION-ORDER BIAS (your own generation-10 finding): when the model names two finalists, the one named FIRST gets ~+1.2 logits (swap test on 53 pair statements), and gold wins 15/15 as the earlier-named letter but 14/27 as the later one. Four L20 heads attend to the first-named letter but zeroing them does NOT reduce the effect. Find the causal circuit: run the swap probes with all attention layers recorded, ablate heads or mixer outputs layer by layer (and conv layers: the short convolutions also carry positional information), and localise what writes the first-named preference. Then remove it so the evidence decides, and show in a read pass on the SAME swap texts that the swap effect shrinks while P(gold) does not fall. Also check whether the same bias acts EARLIER in the trace (the option discussed first in the sweep vs later), since generation 10 showed the conclusion is fixed before the finalists are named."}

{"claude": "LATENT KNOWLEDGE THAT IS LOST (\"knows but does not say\"). Generations 10-11 showed visible reasoning habits are symptoms; look instead for cases where the network internally prefers the RIGHT option and a specific later component overrides it. Concretely: on MIXED and WRONG traces, take forced-answer probes ('So the answer is (') at several points of the thinking and read them through the layers (logit lens on the residual stream at L12-L23 projected onto the option letters, or per-layer direct attribution). Look for a systematic pattern: gold ranked higher at an intermediate layer than at the output, and one or a few late components (an MLP neuron group, a head, a direction) that push it down, e.g. by favouring the option already named most often, the familiar-sounding one, or the model's pre-thinking prior. If such an override exists and is content-independent, weaken it and show on HELD-OUT prefixes (not used to fit) that P(gold) rises before spending generate passes. If no override exists (gold is never preferred internally on wrong traces), say so clearly: that is an important negative result.", "ed_f": "OPEN CHOICE. You are a new editor this generation (no earlier reports of your own). Read the history in this file first: four mechanism-targeted edits in generations 10-11 were real but did not move accuracy, and the noise floor is about +/-4 points. Pick the target you judge most likely to raise P(gold) on held-out probes, and justify the choice in notes.md before spending passes. Candidates the other editors suggested but did not test: (a) replace a hedging or exam-gaming paragraph with a neutral content paragraph in fixed traces and see if P(gold) moves (cause vs symptom); (b) act at the SOURCE of the generic 'first item of a list' feature (the residual direction written at list items) rather than in one head; (c) a gate on uncertainty that steers toward re-deriving content ('Let us recall the definition...') rather than suppressing words; (d) anything else the evidence points to, e.g. option-content comparison errors on two-finalist questions, or the 21 never-right questions if some of them are reasoning slips rather than missing knowledge. Apply the gate rule: show P(gold) rises on held-out prefixes before you generate."}

{"claude": "SELF-CORRECTION. Does the network notice its own wrong steps? Build matched pairs from practice traces: a clean reasoning prefix, and the same prefix with ONE step corrupted (a number, sign, unit or negation changed so the step is false). In teacher-forced read passes, measure what follows the corrupted step vs the clean one: P of re-check tokens ('Wait', 'Actually', 'Let me double-check'), and residual-stream directions that separate corrupted from clean at the step end (fit on some pairs, test on held-out pairs). Then ask whether the signal REACHES the behaviour: in the parent's own wrong traces (pass@4 bank), is the error signal present at the first wrong step but not followed by a re-check? If there is a real detector whose link to re-checking is weak, strengthen that link (only when the detector fires; raising re-checking everywhere is a global knob and out of scope) and show on held-out corrupted pairs that detection->re-check rises while clean steps are left alone. Then test generated conclusions on mixed pass@4 questions. If the network has no error signal, say so clearly: that is an important negative result.", "ed_f": "STEP-LEVEL REASONING ERRORS. Use the pass@4 bank at 8,192 (same question, right and wrong samples). For each finished WRONG sample of a mixed question, find the FIRST false step and classify it (false fact recalled; arithmetic/algebra slip; number or condition copied wrongly from the question; NOT/EXCEPT/units/sign lost; formula or definition misapplied; unsupported leap), and note what the right samples did at the same point. Check that the most frequent class holds on a larger set before spending passes on it (your gen-12 diagnosis did not replicate at 256 questions). Pick the class that is most frequent AND has a findable cause; localise the cause with teacher-forced read passes (e.g. at the error token: which heads attend to the source in the question, which MLP neurons write the wrong value; compare with right samples at the same point), edit it, and show on held-out texts that P(correct step) rises relative to P(wrong step) before you generate. Arithmetic or copying slips are a good place to start if they are frequent, because they also matter for GSM8K."}
